name: regex (Rust regex crate)
baseline: PCRE2 (interpreter and JIT) and RE2 (C/C++ regex engines); Hyperscan also measured
workload: rebar curated barometer: about 38 regex search benchmarks (literals, alternations, dates, Unicode classes, bounded repeats, dictionaries, ReDoS-style patterns, noseyparker rules) across many engines; corroborated by the LangArena Etc::LogParser task (13 log-grep patterns over generated web-server log lines).
claimed_speedup: rebar README summary of search-time benchmarks (geometric mean of per-benchmark speed ratios to the best engine, lower is better): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 1.12.2 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 10.47 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). Compile-time summary goes the other way: pcre2 1.41, pcre2/jit 6.20, rust/regex 11.85, re2 12.28. Intersection computed from the repo's recorded rebar CSVs for 2025-12-19 (derived from repo data, not stated on the page): vs PCRE2 JIT rust/regex is faster in 21 of 34 search benchmarks, geometric mean time ratio 2.13x; vs RE2 faster in 27 of 31, 4.3x; vs PCRE2 interpreter faster in 32 of 33, 44x; vs Hyperscan faster in only 12 of 28 (Hyperscan about 1.45x faster overall). LangArena results 2026-10-05, Etc::LogParser: Rust 0.302 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 0.485 s (clang) and 0.488 s (gcc), about 1.6x, and vs C++ 0.99 s. Same file, Template::Regex ({{(.*?)}} replacement): Rust 3.699 s vs C PCRE2 JIT 1.173 s, so PCRE2 JIT is about 3.2x faster there.
compiler_and_flags: rebar README gives engine versions (rust/regex 1.12.2, pcre2 10.47, re2 2025-11-05) but no compiler flags. LangArena: rustc 1.99.0 'cargo build --release' (opt-level 3), regex 1.12; C side clang 22.1.8 / gcc 16.0.1 with -O2 -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, system PCRE2 with pcre2_jit_compile.
hardware: rebar README does not state the machine. LangArena results file: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 78 GB.
why_faster: rebar analysis: finite-automata engines (lazy DFA, one-pass DFA) with SIMD literal prefilters (memchr, Teddy) avoid backtracking and give DFA-speed matching on most patterns; PCRE2 JIT stays faster where JIT-compiled backtracking is cheap (small anchored patterns, capture-heavy cases).
stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars; the regex engine behind ripgrep and much of the Rust ecosystem
tradeoffs: No backreferences or look-around (linear-time guarantee in exchange). Pattern compilation is slower than PCRE2 and RE2. Unicode tables add binary size. Rust API; C++ needs the rure C binding or FFI.
caveats: The rebar summary geometric means are over different benchmark subsets per engine (28 to 38), so only the intersection numbers are like for like; those were derived by me from the repo's recorded CSVs. rebar is written by the regex crate's author and its README says the analysis is biased towards that crate (BIAS.md). Hyperscan beats it overall and PCRE2 JIT wins roughly a third of the benchmarks. rebar README gives no CPU. The LangArena run is independent but its C side builds with -O2 and hand-written glue, and both implementations differ in surrounding code. Template::Regex shows a 3.2x loss to PCRE2 JIT.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust crate "faster than glibc" string search OR strstr OR strtod OR memmem benchmark SIMD' surfaced memchr and rebar; then opened rebar README (raw.githubusercontent.com) and its record/curated/2025-12-19 CSVs, and kostya/LangArena results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js (https://github.com/kostya/LangArena/blob/master/results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js).

name: memchr (Rust crate, memmem)
baseline: libc memmem (system libc, presumably glibc, called through FFI by rebar's libc engine); libc memchr for single-byte search
workload: Substring search (memmem) over 54 rebar benchmarks (English, Russian and Chinese subtitle and Sherlock haystacks, common/rare/never needles, long and short), oneshot and prebuilt searcher; plus single-byte memchr over 15 benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: No glibc comparison appears in the README (it compares against Rust std: memmem prebuilt geometric mean speed ratio 1.03 vs 6.50, oneshot 1.04 vs 5.26). Derived from the repo's recorded rebar CSV benchmarks/record/x86_64/2023-08-26.csv (memchr 2.5.0), not stated on the README page: libc memmem oneshot vs memchr memmem oneshot geometric mean time ratio 2.0x over 54 benchmarks, memchr faster in 41; libc memmem vs memchr prebuilt searcher 2.83x, memchr faster in 48 of 54 (worst case libc 3x faster, best case memchr 28x faster). Single-byte search is not a win: libc memchr is about 6% faster by geometric mean (memchr crate faster in only 2 of 15).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (Rust release build, rustc nightly 1.73 per README rank output; libc engine is a Rust harness calling libc through FFI).
why_faster: README: forward substring search picks Rabin-Karp for tiny haystacks, a 'Generic SIMD' variant that uses a byte-frequency heuristic to choose rare bytes for small needles, and Two-Way with a SIMD prefilter otherwise; AVX2 chosen at runtime. The README explains the gap to Rust std, not to glibc.
stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars; dependency of the regex crate and ripgrep
tradeoffs: Pure Rust API (&[u8]); from C++ needs FFI. Runtime CPU detection needs the std feature for AVX2, otherwise SSE2 only. The 'prebuilt' searcher API is where most of the gain over libc comes from, which libc's memmem cannot express.
caveats: The libc ratios are my derivation from a CSV in the repo, recorded by the crate author in 2023 on an unrecorded machine with unrecorded libc version; the README never claims a win over glibc. libc memmem is called one-shot, so the comparison includes searcher construction, which favours the crate's prebuilt API when reused. Single-byte memchr shows no advantage over libc.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust crate "faster than glibc" string search OR strstr OR strtod OR memmem benchmark SIMD'; opened memchr README and benchmarks/engines.toml and the recorded CSV.

name: sd (find and replace CLI)
baseline: GNU sed (C), sed -E and plain sed; version not stated
workload: Replace a quote character on about 1.5 GB of JSON; regex replacement (\w+) -> $1$1 on a 55 MB JSON file; literal and regex replacement line-by-line vs across-lines mode on a 36 MB, 1M-line file.
claimed_speedup: README, hyperfine means: simple replacement on ~1.5 GB JSON: sed -E 2.338 s, sed 2.365 s, sd 0.997 s (~2.35 times faster). Regex replacement on a ~55 MB JSON: sed -E 11.315 s, sed 11.239 s, sd 0.942 s (~11.93 times faster). 1M lines (~36 MB): sd -A 'foo' 125.6 ms, sed 316.4 ms, default sd (line-by-line) 357.0 ms, so sed is about 1.13x faster than default-mode sd on a literal; regex '(\w+) world': sd -A 254.0 ms, sd default 566.7 ms, sed -E 4432.7 ms (about 7.8x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Different syntax (JavaScript/Python-style regex, $1 captures), not a full sed (no scripting, addresses or hold space). Default line-by-line mode keeps memory at 3 MB; across mode (-A) is faster but used 74 MB peak RSS on the 36 MB test.
caveats: First-party README numbers, no CPU, OS, sed version, locale or build flags. Command lines are public but the 1.5 GB and 55 MB JSON inputs are not provided. GNU sed regex speed depends on locale (UTF-8 vs C), unstated. The README itself calls the syntax examples cherry-picked. sd uses the Rust regex crate while GNU sed uses glibc regex, so large regex gaps are engine differences; literal replacement in default mode is slower than sed.
found_via: Cross-check while searching text-processing CLIs; opened README via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com/chmln/sd page and commits feed.

name: jumprope (Rust rope)
baseline: librope (C skip-list rope by the same author)
workload: Replaying real text-editing traces (automerge-paper, rustcode, sveltecomponent, seph-blog1) from crdt-benchmarks against a rope: insert/delete at arbitrary positions.
claimed_speedup: README table, single core of a Ryzen 5800X: automerge-paper librope (C) 16.28 ms vs Jumprope 6.66 ms; rustcode 3.93 vs 1.66 ms; sveltecomponent 1.59 vs 0.59 ms; seph-blog1 10.01 vs 3.81 ms (about 2.4x to 2.7x, derived from page data). README also says jumprope is about 3x faster than ropey (a Rust rope) on real editing operations, and its JumpRopeBuf wrapper (merges runs of edits before applying them) is claimed about 10x faster again.
why_faster: README: jumprope is a skip list whose leaf nodes each contain a gap buffer, versus librope's plain skip list.
tradeoffs: Fewer features than ropey (no line/column conversion). Meant for large documents; the README recommends std String for strings under about 100 bytes.
caveats: First-party numbers from the author, who also wrote the C baseline; flags for librope (C compiler and optimisation level) are not stated, and the algorithms differ (gap-buffer leaves), so the gap is design plus language. Full Criterion report is on the author's site (not opened). Repo has no commits since 2023-05-20.
found_via: Searched for text-buffer and rope libraries with a C baseline; opened README via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com page and commits feed.

name: Vibrato (Rust MeCab reimplementation)
workload: Tokenizing 2,346 sentences (average 158.8 characters) of 'I Am a Cat' by Soseki Natsume with mecab-ipadic 2.7.0 and unidic-cwj 3.1.1 dictionaries, averaged over 100 runs.
claimed_speedup: Wiki Speed-Comparison table: Vibrato 0.5.0 ipadic 42 ms vs MeCab ipadic 87 ms (about 2.1x, derived from page data); Vibrato unidic-cwj 75 ms vs MeCab unidic-cwj 179 ms (about 2.4x, derived from page data); the Vibrato raw-connector variant takes 1364 ms (7.6x slower than MeCab) and dual-connector 170 ms (about equal).
hardware: Intel Core i9-12900K, 64 GB DDR5, Ubuntu 22.04
why_faster: README: reimplementation of the MeCab algorithm simplified and optimised; for dictionaries with a large connection matrix (unidic-cwj, 459 MiB) cache-efficient id mappings make it faster.
tradeoffs: Rust library, C++ needs FFI or the CLI. Uses its own compiled dictionary format (zstd compressed system.dic.zst), converted from MeCab dictionaries; MeCab-compatible output options exist.
caveats: First-party wiki page; compiler and flags not stated, MeCab build flags not stated, single corpus of one novel, one machine. The raw-connector configuration is slower than MeCab. Speedup is largest with the large-matrix unidic dictionary. The wiki page is the only source opened; the figure on the README (figures/comparison.svg) was not read.
found_via: Searched for Rust reimplementations with a C++ baseline (tokenizers); opened vibrato README and its Speed-Comparison wiki page.

name: Sassy (SIMD approximate string matching)
baseline: Edlib (C++ Myers bit-vector aligner); parasail (C) and SWOffinder also compared in the paper
workload: Searching short DNA/ASCII patterns (up to about 1000 characters) in long texts allowing k edit errors, synthetic data and a human genome search.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract as returned in a WebSearch snippet (the bioRxiv page itself is blocked here): 4x to 15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp, text throughput near 2 Gbp/s, over 100x faster than parasail, 100x faster than SWOffinder on CRISPR off-target search. Repo README: version 2 is 2x faster on AVX-512 and pre-encoding patterns is 10-20x faster for short texts (these are internal comparisons).
compiler_and_flags: README: build with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' (AVX2 or NEON needed); Edlib build flags not seen.
why_faster: Bit-packing with SIMD (AVX2/NEON) where the bit-vectors run along the text direction ('tiling in the text direction'), with the text split into 4 parts searched in parallel; complexity O(k ceil(n/W)) with W=256.
stars_or_usage: 169 stars; published on crates.io, bioconda and PyPI (sassy-rs)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 or NEON; supports ASCII, DNA and IUPAC alphabets; best for patterns up to about 1000; C bindings, Python bindings and a CLI exist.
caveats: Numbers come from the paper abstract as quoted in a search snippet (snippet only); the preprint, the Bioinformatics article (doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag244, listed on the README) and the eval CSVs were not opened. Edlib uses no explicit SIMD, so the comparison pits AVX2 against a scalar-word Myers implementation. The README itself never states the Edlib ratio. Repository evals/ directory has the harness (run_tool_bench.py) so a reproduction is possible.
found_via: WebSearch 'Sassy SIMD approximate string matching DNA Rust faster than Edlib speedup'; opened README, evals/README.md and repo page.

name: A*PA2 (astar-pairwise-aligner)
baseline: Edlib (C++) and BiWFA / WFA2-lib (C) exact global aligners
workload: Exact global pairwise alignment (edit distance) of long DNA sequences, e.g. ONT reads of a human genome with 6% to 11% divergence, plus synthetic sequences.
claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'up to 20x speedup over other exact aligners and is competitive with approximate aligners'. Paper abstract as quoted in a WebSearch snippet (WABI 2024, LIPIcs 312, paper page blocked): 19x faster than BiWFA and Edlib on >500 kbp ONT reads at 6% divergence; 5.6x at 11 kbp reads with 11% divergence; 0.81x (slower) on 800 bp reads at 11% divergence; A*PA2-simple is 6x to 8x faster than Edlib for sequences of at least 10 kbp.
why_faster: Per the paper snippet: like Edlib it uses Ukkonen band doubling with Myers bit-packing, adding large blocks, SIMD, a new profile and the A* heuristics from A*PA (a different algorithm, not a language effect).
tradeoffs: Gains only on long, low-divergence inputs; slower than Edlib on short, highly divergent reads. Latest commit message mentions 'latest nightly', so a nightly Rust toolchain may be needed (not confirmed). MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft. Evaluation harness lives in a separate pa-bench repo.
caveats: Only the 'up to 20x' README sentence was verified on a page I opened; the 19x, 5.6x and 0.81x figures are snippet only from the peer-reviewed paper. CPU and flags not found. Pairwise alignment is on the edge of the string-and-text category.
found_via: WebSearch 'A*PA2 exact global sequence alignment Rust faster than Edlib WFA github astarpa2'; opened the repo page and commits feed.

name: eBay TSV Utilities (D)
baseline: GNU awk 4.2.1, mawk 1.3.3, GNU cut 8.25 and GNU Datamash 1.3 (all C)
workload: Six command-line tasks on multi-GB delimited text: numeric row filter and regex row filter (4.8 GB / 2.7 GB), column selection (wide and narrow lines), file join, summary statistics, CSV-to-TSV; also compared with xsv (Rust) and csvtk (Go).
claimed_speedup: 2018 study, Linux (16-CPU Haswell cloud machine), seconds: numeric row filter tsv-filter 5.48 vs mawk 11.31 vs GNU awk 42.80 (about 2.1x and 7.8x, derived from page data); column selection (4.8 GB) tsv-select 4.79 vs mawk 9.51 vs GNU cut 14.46 (about 3.0x vs cut); summary statistics tsv-summarize 15.78 vs GNU Datamash 48.51 (about 3.1x); regex row filter tsv-filter 8.80 vs mawk 17.74 vs GNU awk 29.02, but xsv (Rust) 7.97 is faster; narrow-line column selection (86M short lines) GNU cut 5.60 beats tsv-select 8.26. A third-party README (hck) on a Ryzen 9 3950X shows tsv-select 1.702 s vs GNU cut 8.30 at 7.541 s (about 4.4x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: tsv-utils v1.1.19 built with LDC with LTO and PGO (2018 notes); C comparison tools (GNU awk, mawk, GNU cut, GNU Datamash) are standard package-manager binaries with unknown flags.
hardware: Linux: 16 CPU Intel Haswell 2095 MHz, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04; MacOS: Mac mini 3 GHz Intel i7
why_faster: Author's stated reasons: straightforward D with avoidance of GC allocation, LDC link-time and profile-guided optimisation (2018 gain), TSV-only data model (no CSV escape handling, which the docs call computationally more expensive); the tools are single-threaded, so none of the gain is from parallelism.
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars; prebuilt Linux and macOS binaries
tradeoffs: TSV-only (no CSV escapes except csv2tsv); a toolkit of single-purpose tools rather than awk-like scripting; D toolchain needed to build.
caveats: First-party 2018 study (data now 8 years old); the author frames it as a test of D against C, Go and Rust but the comparison tools are not exact equivalents and the D side uses LTO plus PGO while C tools are distro binaries (unmatched optimisation). GNU cut wins the narrow-line benchmark and xsv wins regex filtering. Repo has no commits since 2021-06-13. The 4.4x figure comes from a competitor's README (hck), where the cut version is 8.30.
found_via: QUEUE.md cross-wave lead 'eBay/tsv-utils'; opened README, docs/Performance.md, docs/comparative-benchmarks-2018.md and the hck README benchmark table.

name: needletail (Rust FASTA/FASTQ parser)
workload: Parsing a 4-line FASTQ file of 5,682,010 records and counting records, sequence length and quality length; plain and gzip-compressed input.
claimed_speedup: lh3/biofast README, fqcnt table (CPU seconds): needletail plain 0.8 s vs C kseq.h 1.4 s (1.75x, derived from page data); gzip input 9.3 s vs 9.7 s (about equal; decompression dominates).
compiler_and_flags: Setup lists gcc-4.8.5 for the C side; Rust toolchain version and flags not stated in the README.
hardware: CentOS 7 server with two EPYC 7301 CPUs and 1 TB memory
tradeoffs: Rust API (no C++ binding in repo). Parses FASTA and 4-line FASTQ only, while the baseline kseq.h also handles multi-line records, which the biofast table marks in its comments column.
caveats: Independent benchmark by the author of kseq.h, but from 2020, with the needletail version not stated; gzip time is dominated by decompression and shows no gain. Different feature scope (4-line only) makes the comparison favour needletail. Needletail's own README claims only 'as fast as the readfq C library'. Crystal, Nim and Julia ports of kseq.h do not beat C in the same table.
found_via: Searched for cross-language text-parsing shootouts; opened lh3/biofast README (fqcnt table) and needletail repo page and commits feed.

name: fastgrep (Rust grep)
workload: Recursive searches over a generated corpus of 200 files x 5,000 lines of Rust-like source (sparse and dense matches, case-insensitive, regex, single 100k-line file) and a scaling test of 50 to 500 files.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark table (warm trigram index, LC_ALL=C): -rn 'fn main' 8.82 ms vs GNU grep 32.99 ms (3.74x); -rc 'use ' 8.55 ms vs 84.75 ms (9.91x); -rni error 37.49 ms vs 82.57 ms (2.20x); -rn 'impl\s+Drop' 45.24 vs 73.43 (1.62x); very sparse SubscriptionManager 5.41 vs 39.35 (7.28x); single file 3.70 vs 5.21 (1.41x); but -rl 'fn main' 7.50 ms vs GNU grep 7.12 ms (0.95x, GNU grep faster). Scaling: 1.48x at 50 files, 2.43x at 200, 3.08x at 500.
compiler_and_flags: fastgrep 0.1.9, Rust 1.99.0 release build, Criterion benchmarks; GNU grep 3.12 installed via Homebrew (build flags unknown).
hardware: Apple M2 Max (12 logical CPUs), 32 GB, macOS 27.0.1
why_faster: README: parallel by default across all CPU threads, lazy trigram index that skips non-matching files on repeat searches, SIMD-accelerated literal search.
tradeoffs: Output order is non-deterministic (multi-threaded); deliberate deviations from GNU grep (binary files, long lines). Index cache stored under the OS cache directory and invalidated by mtime and size. Not every GNU grep flag implemented.
caveats: Very new project, first-party numbers. Gains come mostly from 12-thread parallelism and a warm index versus single-threaded GNU grep, not from a faster per-byte scan; the README itself notes --no-index is often faster when the index cannot skip files. Synthetic corpus, small (about 1M lines) so process start-up matters. GNU grep was run on macOS via Homebrew with LC_ALL=C.
found_via: WebSearch 'Go OR Zig OR Nim OR Odin text processing library "faster than" C PCRE2 OR strstr OR "GNU grep" OR "GNU sed" benchmark github 2025' surfaced fastgrep; opened README via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com page and commits feed.

name: hck (Rust cut replacement)
workload: Selecting fields 1, 8 and 19 from a 7-million-line CSV (all_train.csv) with a single-character delimiter, and from a multi-space delimited variant.
claimed_speedup: README hyperfine means (7M-line CSV): hck -Ld, 1.198 s, hck -d, 1.649 s, GNU cut -d, 7.541 s +- 1.250 (6.3x and 4.6x, taken from the Relative column and derived), awk (mawk 1.3.4 listed) 4.993 s, tsv-select 1.702 s, xsv 5.693 s, choose 4.285 s. Multi-character delimiter (space runs): hck -Ld'   ' 1.718 s vs `tr -s ' ' | cut` 7.471 s (4.3x, different pipelines), while `tr -s ' ' | hck -Ld' '` takes 6.171 s (1.2x faster than `tr | cut`) because tr dominates.
compiler_and_flags: hck, xsv, choose and tsv-utils compiled locally 'with optimizations' (README); GNU cut 8.30 from Ubuntu 20 packages.
hardware: Ubuntu 20, AMD Ryzen 9 3950X 16-core, 64 GB DDR4, NVMe
tradeoffs: Regex or literal multi-character delimiters and column reordering that cut lacks; offers memory-mapped input (the --no-mmap rows are 13% to 28% slower); regex delimiters are about 4x to 6x slower than literal ones.
caveats: The README says the benchmarks are 'not authoritative' and only meant to show hck is in the same ballpark; first-party; GNU cut 8.30 is slower than awk on this input, which is unusual, and its row has a +-1.25 s spread; the cause was not examined. Local optimised builds on one side against distro packages on the other. No mechanism stated by the source.
found_via: Found while reading the hck README table that also lists tsv-utils (searching text-processing CLIs with GNU baselines).
